SYSTEMS PROGRAMMING AND MACHINE ORGANIZATION
Chapter 33 — Files
VERBATIM GRADUATE LECTURE TRANSCRIPT
Charles Dorner

SLIDE 1: Chapter 33 — Files

LECTURE NARRATION
A file interface presents data through a persistent name, an open handle, or a stream-like endpoint. The operating system hides many device details, but the abstraction does not make every endpoint behave like a seekable array of bytes. Correct I/O code begins by identifying which guarantees the particular object provides. The Linux/POSIX examples distinguish a pathname , an underlying filesystem object, an open file description , and a process’s file descriptor . Those are related objects, not four names for the same thing. The distinction explains shared offsets, inherited descriptors, and why removing a pathname need not immediately invalidate an already-open handle. [ R47 , R13 ]

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a file interface presents data through a persistent name, an open handle, or a stream-like endpoint.

SLIDE 4: 33.1 Regular files

LECTURE NARRATION
A regular file provides byte-oriented contents and metadata under filesystem rules. It usually supports seeking to a position and reading or writing there. Its logical size need not equal the amount of physical storage allocated, as sparse regions illustrate. A pathname is a route through a directory namespace, not a permanent guarantee about object identity. Another process can rename or replace an entry between separate pathname operations. When an operation must apply to the object already opened, use the descriptor and descriptor-relative interfaces where appropriate rather than reopening the name and assuming it still denotes the same object.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

========================================================================================

SLIDE 6: 33.2 Streams

LECTURE NARRATION
A stream exposes an ordered flow of bytes or records according to its interface. Pipes and TCP sockets are byte streams that do not support arbitrary seeking. Data may arrive gradually, and a read can return fewer bytes than requested. The C standard-I/O concept of a stream adds buffering and library state through FILE* . That is another layer: a FILE* may wrap a regular file or another supported endpoint. Distinguish the endpoint’s capabilities from the library abstraction used to access it.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a stream exposes an ordered flow of bytes or records according to its interface.

SLIDE 8: 33.3 Random-access files

LECTURE NARRATION
Random access means that the program can select positions rather than consume data only in arrival order. A file format can use fixed-size records, an index, or offsets into variable-length data. The format must define byte ordering, field widths, and bounds independently of a compiler’s in-memory structure layout. Seeking past the end does not itself write intervening bytes. Subsequent writes can extend the file according to filesystem semantics. A robust parser checks offsets and lengths against the actual file size before accessing a region, using subtraction-based bounds checks that avoid overflowing offset + length .

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

SLIDE 10: 33.4 File position

LECTURE NARRATION
An open file description maintains a current file offset for interfaces such as read , write , and lseek on seekable objects. Descriptors created by dup or inherited through fork can refer to the same open file description and therefore share that offset. Separate open calls generally create separate open file descriptions, even when the pathname identifies the same file. Their current offsets are independent. Positional I/O such as pread and pwrite specifies an offset for an operation without using the shared current position in the same way, making it useful for independent random access.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

SLIDE 12: 33.5 Metadata

LECTURE NARRATION
Metadata describes properties such as type, size, permissions, ownership, and timestamps. Descriptor-based inspection identifies the already-open object. A metadata result is a snapshot, not a lock that prevents later changes by another process. Security-sensitive code should avoid checking a pathname and then assuming the checked property remains true during a later open. This is a time-of-check/time-of-use problem. Use interfaces and ownership rules that bind validation to the actual object being used, and account for concurrent modification when the application permits it.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, metadata describes properties such as type, size, permissions, ownership, and timestamps.

SLIDE 14: Worked example — Record boundaries without overflow

LECTURE NARRATION
Suppose a file format begins with a 16-byte header followed by fixed 24-byte records. A file of 160 bytes contains (160 - 16) / 24 = 6 complete records, with no trailing bytes. Record 4, using zero-based indexing, begins at 16 + 4 × 24 = 112 and occupies bytes 112 through 135. A safe validation sequence first requires file_size >= header_size . It then computes payload_size = file_size - header_size , verifies that payload_size % record_size == 0 , and derives the record count. Only after checking index < record_count should it form the selected record’s offset. For an arbitrary byte range with offset o and length n , prefer: This avoids computing an unchecked sum that could wrap. The checks establish a valid range in the observed file size; they do not prevent another process from truncating the file afterward. The application needs an immutability or coordination policy when concurrent modification is possible.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, suppose a file format begins with a 16-byte header followed by fixed 24-byte records.

SLIDE 16: Worked example — Sequential versus random file access

LECTURE NARRATION
Reading a 1 MiB file from beginning to end advances the file offset naturally after each read. To revisit byte 100 without rereading earlier bytes, a seekable regular file can use lseek to reposition before reading. Pipes and terminals are streams and generally do not support arbitrary seek semantics.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SLIDE 18: Worked example — Metadata is not file content

LECTURE NARRATION
A file’s permissions, owner, timestamps, and size are metadata. Reading file data does not automatically reveal all metadata, and changing metadata does not necessarily change file bytes. Systems code often uses separate interfaces such as stat to query this information.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

LECTURE NARRATION
Lab 33. Apply the record checks to file sizes 15, 16, 159, and 160. State which files are structurally valid under the stated format and how many records each valid file contains. Review 1. Why can two descriptors share a file position? Review 2. Why does a successful metadata check not freeze the file?

SLIDE 22: Chapter Synthesis

LECTURE NARRATION
The chapter's central subject is files. Correct reasoning requires explicit assumptions, bounds, ownership, and interface contracts. Observed behavior is evidence about a run; it is not automatically a language or system guarantee. Use the worked examples and lab to test whether the model transfers to new cases.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true.
